sections.title: Introduction to Data Sufficiency
sections.content: Data Sufficiency (DS) questions do not ask you to find the final answer. Instead, they ask whether the provided statements give you enough information to find the answer. Your goal is to evaluate the sufficiency of the data, not to perform the full calculation.

sections.title: The Standard Five Options
sections.content: Almost all DS questions use these 5 options: A) Statement I alone is sufficient. B) Statement II alone is sufficient. C) Either statement alone is sufficient. D) Both statements together are not sufficient. E) Both statements together are necessary.

sections.title: Step 1: Analyze the Question Stem
sections.content: Before looking at the statements, figure out exactly what the question is asking. Is it a 'Value' question (e.g., 'What is x?') or a 'Yes/No' question (e.g., 'Is x even?')? Simplify the question if possible.

sections.title: Step 2: Evaluate Statement I Alone
sections.content: Read only Statement I. Ignore Statement II completely. Ask yourself: 'Using only this information, can I answer the question definitively?'

sections.title: Step 3: Evaluate Statement II Alone
sections.content: Now, forget everything you read in Statement I. Read only Statement II. Ask yourself: 'Using only this information, can I answer the question definitively?'

sections.title: Step 4: Combine ONLY if Necessary
sections.content: If (and only if) BOTH Statement I and Statement II were insufficient on their own, combine the information from both statements. Ask: 'Using both pieces of information together, can I answer the question?'

sections.title: Value Questions Rule
sections.content: For a 'Value' question (e.g., 'How old is Ravi?'), the data is sufficient ONLY if it gives you a single, exact number. If the data gives you multiple possibilities (e.g., 'Ravi is 15 or 16'), it is insufficient.

sections.title: Yes/No Questions Rule
sections.content: For a 'Yes/No' question, the data is sufficient if it gives a definite 'Yes' OR a definite 'No'. A 'Maybe' or 'Sometimes' means the data is insufficient.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Solving the problem completely. 2. Forgetting to evaluate the statements independently (carrying info from I to II). 3. Combining statements too early. 4. Assuming a 'No' answer means the data is insufficient.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In Data Sufficiency, you are a judge evaluating evidence. Evaluate each statement separately. Only combine them if they fail individually. Remember, a definite 'No' is a sufficient answer to a Yes/No question.

tricks.title: The 'Stop Calculation' Rule
tricks.explanation: Stop calculating as soon as you know an answer exists. Do not waste time finding the actual number.
tricks.example: If Statement 1 says 'x + 5 = 10', you know you can find x. You don't need to actually calculate x = 5 to mark it sufficient.

tricks.title: The 'Forgetfulness' Trick
tricks.explanation: When testing Statement II, physically cover Statement I with your hand to prevent accidental data carry-over.
tricks.example: If Statement I says 'x is positive', forget that when reading Statement II.

tricks.title: Definite 'No' = Sufficient
tricks.explanation: For Yes/No questions, if the data proves the answer is definitely 'No', the data IS sufficient.
tricks.example: Q: Is x > 10? Statement: x = 5. Answer is NO. Therefore, the statement is sufficient.

tricks.title: The 'Multiple Answers = Insufficient' Rule
tricks.explanation: If a statement leads to two or more possible answers for a value question, it is always insufficient.
tricks.example: Q: What is x? Statement: x² = 9. x could be 3 or -3. Insufficient.

tricks.title: The A/D vs B/C/E Split
tricks.explanation: If Statement I is sufficient, the answer must be A (I alone) or C (Either). You can immediately eliminate B, D, and E.
tricks.example: This narrows down your choices quickly.
